h2. Threat Scenario

The RI.Insights application APIs use a cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) policy that allows access from any domain. This may allow a third party threat actor to retrieve sensitive data from a session or perform privileged actions on behalf of the user.

h2. Potential Impact

An Internet-based threat actor could target users of the RI.Insightsapplication by embedding script payloads or abusing Cross-Site Scripting vulnerabilities on other, often trusted, websites. When the payload is run in the browser of the target user, it could direct requests to the Cumulus application; if the target user is already authenticated to RI.Insights, the threat actor would be able to covertly issue and retrieve the results of the malicious requests as if they were issued legitimately by the authenticated user.

h2. Threat Discovery

An anonymous Internet-based threat actor could discover this vulnerable condition by sending a request to RI.Insightswith a custom HTTP Origin header containing the domain of their choice. For instance, an attacker could create an HTTP Origin header containing 'Origin: [https://attack.l9group.com|https://attack.l9group.com/]' and then observe the response from the server that appends the chosen domain of the threat actor to the trusted Origin list.

h2. Affected Components

faq-service-Release-2.1-master\src\main\java\org\snn\api\ApiOriginFilter.java

h2. Remediation Recommendation

Create a CORS policy that only allows a trusted list of domains.

h2. Technical Details

The assessment team initially discovered this issue after noting the wildcard Origin HTTP header explicitly set in the API filter source code. To validate the presence of the issue on the provided environment, comprehensive mapping of application assets and API endpoints was conducted. Each discovered asset or endpoint was then actively requested with a provided Origin header containing a wildcard or a domain specified and controlled by the assessment team. Each HTTP response was analyzed to determine how the server platform reacted to the Origin payload and in this case, affirming the source code discovery of the vulnerability, the application server responded with Access-Control-Allow-Origin header containing the wildcard value.

summary: Docker container runs as USER root
description:
h2. Threat Scenario

Multiple runtime dependencies of the application are outdated and one bundled library contains high-risk vulnerabilities. Vulnerabilities that reside deep in dependencies or Third-Party Components (TPCs) typically survive in an application attack surface for extended periods of time. In contrast to vulnerabilities in custom application code, vulnerabilities in TPCs, once discovered publicly, are exploited in large horizontal operations by threat actors. Note that in this case, the affected component is currently listed as End-Of-Life (EOL) from the software vendor and security updates may not be available for this version.

h2. Potential Impact

Containers that do not prevent applications from running as USER root could allow a threat actor who has gained access to the container to run code as a privileged (root) user. Applications running as root in the container that have been exploited could be used by the threat actor to execute commands / actions as the root user via the exploited application.

h2. Threat Discovery

The assessment team examined the affected Docker configuration files and noted that commands are run as the USER root. The USER attribute is not set to a lower privilege user after the commands are run, resulting in the container running with root privileges. A threat actor that has compromised the containerized application could discern the process privilege attained.

h2. Affected Components

s3-java-unzipper-eb-Release-2.1-master\Dockerfile

h2. Remediation Recommendation

After running the required privileged commands as the 'root' user, drop privileges by switching the user context to a normal unprivileged user for running the application.

h2. Technical Details

The assessment team examined the affected Docker configuration files and noted that commands are run as the USER root. The USER attribute is not set to a lower privilege user after the commands are run, resulting in the container running with root privileges.

h2. Threat Scenario

A number of API parameters are vulnerable to backend query injection. The assessment team was able to reliably confirm the existence of these vulnerabilities by asking the database to sleep for a specific period of time after processing the query and then monitoring the response latency, but unable to leverage these vectors for a cybersecurity impact within the time of testing.

h2. Potential Impact

Unknown at this time. The location of the queries and the configuration of the AWS ELB and WAF prevent commonly used methods of exploitation.

h2. Threat Discovery

An authenticated attacker could invest in application mapping and parameter injection to discover the existence of these injection sources, but leveraging them would require significant investment in evasions.

h2. Affected Components

[https://preprod.real-intelligence.com/api/v1/case-service/case/component|https://preprod.real-intelligence.com/api/v1/case-service/case/component] (implant parameter)

h2. Remediation Recommendation

Level Nine recommends expanding the use of Spring DataBinder to strongly type incoming parameters, in the case of the implant parameter, constrain and validate the processed input to the list of Implant names supported by the application.

h2. Technical Details

The assessment team issued a request to the case service with the "implant" parameter including payloads designed to delay the response. For example, the payload "%2b(select*from(select(sleep(15)))a)%2b" is designed to delay the response for 15 seconds and the response to this request took over 15 seconds to complete. This behavior indicates the payload was successfully evaluated server-side.

h2. Threat Scenario

Multiple runtime dependencies of the application are outdated and one bundled library contains high-risk vulnerabilities. Vulnerabilities that reside deep in dependencies or Third-Party Components (TPCs) typically survive in an application attack surface for extended periods of time. In contrast to vulnerabilities in custom application code, vulnerabilities in TPCs, once discovered publicly, are exploited in large horizontal operations by threat actors. Note that in this case, the affected component is currently listed as End-Of-Life (EOL) from the software vendor and security updates may not be available for this version.

h2. Potential Impact

If exploited, a vulnerability in a dependency may put the application at risk, resulting in compromise of the entire application. The assessment team was not able to validate an exploitable path to the dependency vulnerabilities.

summary: Low-Level User can Toggle Activation Status in Admin Panel
description:
h2. Threat Scenario

A threat actor with access as an authenticated RI.Insights user can access an API endpoint which can change visual display state of the "status" indicator in the Users section of the RI.Insights portal.

h2. Potential Impact

A threat actor with knowledge of this API endpoint could toggle the visual "status" display of any user in the system. This could cause users with access to the Users section of the RI.Insights portal to believe that a user has been falsely activated or deactivated in the system. Note that this action does not disable user access to the system, but only changes the visual indicator. Also note that if an Admin "re-enables" the user via the slider, this will trigger a password reset for the affected user.

h2. Threat Discovery

A threat actor could infer the request structure by either capturing it via an on-path (e.g. MITM) attack or constructing the request with reasonable understanding of the website functionality.

h2. Affected Components

[preprod.real-intelligence.com/api/v1/users-service/user/useraction|http://preprod.real-intelligence.com/api/v1/users-service/user/useraction]

h2. Remediation Recommendation

Implement proper access control on all administrator/high-level functions. Verify the status of each user in the back end of the website as well.

h2. Technical Details

When logged into the RI.Insights application as a user with Administrator permissions, the assessment team reviewed API calls made by the browser to the various RI.Insights API endpoints. The assessment team observed an API call to the /api/v1/users-service/user/useraction API endpoint when enabling or disabling a user account in the system, which included the action (enabled: true or enabled: false), and the User ID of the targeted user. The assessment team then authenticated to the system as a non-privileged user (surgeon and care team member), and using the Authorization Bearer token, re-issued the call to the useraction API. Note that this action could be performed against any user, assuming their User ID were known. The assessment team observed that, in the Users UI when logged in as an Administrator, the status of the user would change to the state issued by the non-privileged user's API call. This action did not enable or disable the targeted user, however it did affect the UI of the administrator, which could prove confusing to the admin. Further, the assessment team observed that if the Administrative user re-enabled a user after being set to disabled, this would trigger a password reset for the targeted user.

h2. Threat Scenario

Any authenticated user can forge logs generated from the web client to the logger service. A threat actor can abuse this ability to falsify application logs, submit excessive invalid logs, and undermine nonrepudiation of logged activity.

h2. Potential Impact

A threat actor with knowledge of this vulnerability could falsify log data as it is sent from the client to the logger service. A threat actor could also leverage this vulnerability to flood logs with superfluous data.

h2. Threat Discovery

A threat actor with an authenticated session to the application can note issued requests to "logger-service" and observe that the requests contain a "UserId" field which may be modified.

h2. Affected Components

[preprod.real-intelligence.com/api/v1/logger-service/logger|http://preprod.real-intelligence.com/api/v1/logger-service/logger]

h2. Remediation Recommendation

Level Nine recommends that Smith and Nephew validate inputs submitted to the website logger; associated user IDs should be validated or set by identifying the user associated with the authenticated session being utilized for the request. Additionally, where possible logging should be implemented server-side to minimize client/user control of log contents.

h2. Technical Details

The assessment team observed requests to "logger-service" containing a "UserId" field. The team issued additional requests to the logger-service containing forged/modified fields. Subsequent review of activity logs in the application showed that the user ID was successfully forged.

h2. Threat Scenario

When an account is deactivated any preexisting authenticated session for that account remains functional. A authenticated session will stay active until it times out or the user logs out. If an account is deactivated in response to a threat actor gaining access, the threat actor could continue to access account functionality with a preexisting authenticated session.

h2. Potential Impact

The threat actor with a preexisting authenticated session to an account can continue to abuse data and functionality in the account even after the account has been deactivated.

h2. Threat Discovery

A threat actor does not need knowledge of this weakness to abuse it. If the threat actor has a preexisting authenticated session to the application, they may continue to utilize the session after account deactivation.

h2. Affected Components

Ri.INSIGHTS

h2. Remediation Recommendation

Level Nine recommends Smith and Nephew invalidate a user's current session(s) immediately upon account deactivation.

h2. Technical Details

The assessment team logged into the application as an Admin user in one browser and any other user in another browser. The user account was deactivated by the Admin account. Subsequently, the user could continue to use the preexisting authenticated session to interact with the application.

summary: Denial of Service through Resource Consumption
description:
h2. Threat Scenario

The assessment team observed that, if many devices are created in a short period of time, the RI.Insights application becomes unresponsive. A threat-actor with admin privileges can flood the application with device creation operations to consume excessive resources and affect the availability of the application.

h2. Potential Impact

A threat actor can flood the application with device creation requests to cause excessive consumption of application resources and result in a Denial of Service (DoS) attack.

h2. Threat Discovery

A threat actor which has gained Admin privileges can observe the ability to create new devices in the Admin panel. The threat actor may infer that creating a device results in a resource consumption, that if repeatedly executed, could affect application availability.

h2. Affected Components

[preprod.real-intelligence.com/api/v1/users-service/deviceinfo|http://preprod.real-intelligence.com/api/v1/users-service/deviceinfo]

h2. Remediation Recommendation

Level Nine recommends that Smith & Nephew enforce a rate limit for all functionality which may result in adverse resource consumption. Do this for all users including high privilege users such as administrators.

h2. Technical Details

The assessment team issued many device creation requests. Each request incremented the "serialno" value in the request body such that each request created a new device. Initially, the requests completed successfully returning an HTTP 200 status code. Though, after approximately 1 minute, the assessment team also noticed that the requests started returning 500 "Internal Server Error" and 502 "Bad Gateway" responses which indicate application availability was impacted.

As a surgeon, I would want to know the how jump distance changes along the liner circumference to maximize joint stability, especially when planning lipped or anteverted liners.

* A view of the cup opening should be provided, with labels to indicate anterior (A), posterior (P), lateral (L), and medial (M) directions.

A drop-down menu should provide the option to modify lip orientation (i.e., switch between the different “o’clock” positions). 
*  Jump distance is defined as the distance the femoral head needs to travel before dislocating after impingement occurred. It is a purely geometric feature that mostly depends on the height of the liner. When lipped or anteverted liners are used, lip height progressively changes throughout the liner circumference, reaching its peak at the lip apex and at the opposite side of the apex. Therefore jump distance should be depicted by color-coding the liner circumference and with a legend indicating max and min jump distance for the selected liner. 
* The cup opening view where jump distance is depicted should also be used to display more cleanly the implant-on-implant impingement areas. summary: Enable new TKA implants to be compatible with Surgeon Personalized Planning
description:
With the Release of CORI 2.0, with the introduction of a implantdefaults.json file, any new TKA implant that is added to an IDB after the CORI 2.0 release, will NOT be compatible with Surgeon Personalized Planning (SPP). 

This is because there are 7 reference values that are required to be set for a specific implant design (and deformity bucket) which are not all provided by the IDB (which is what led to the introduction of the implantdefaults.json to enable the SPP feature in CORI 2.0).

The 7 preference values for a *Varus* preoperative deformity are:

# Femur component V/v
# Femur distal _lateral_ resection
# Femur posterior medial resection
# Femur posterior lateral resection
# Tibia component V/v
# Tibia component slope
# Tibia _lateral_ resection

The 7 preference values for a *Valgus* preoperative deformity are:

# Femur component V/v
# Femur distal _medial_ resection
# Femur posterior medial resection
# Femur posterior lateral resection
# Tibia component V/v
# Tibia component slope
# Tibia _medial_ resection

The only preference values that could be pulled directly from the IDB FM0049 (for a particular implant) are:

# Femur component V/v
# Tibia component V/v
# Tibia component slope
# Tibia lateral resection

Thus, as part of the CORI 2.0 project the implantdefaults.json was created to fill in these missing values.  These default values were provided by the Marketing Team for each of the 9 TKA implants compatible with CORI that existed at the time of the CORI 2.0 project. The defaults provided were based on manual surgical technique as specified in the S+N implant surgical technique guides. The 9 implants are:

# Journey II XR
# Journey II CR
# Journey II BCS
# Legion CR
# Legion PS
# Genesis II PS
# Genesis II CR
# Anthem PS
# Legion Porous CR

If a future TKA implant is added to a CORI IDB, that implant will NOT be compatible with SPP without a Software Update.

The CORI 2.0 brainstormed potential partial solutions to mitigate this, but all options introduced technical debt and had the potential to be confusing for end users so none were pursued. These partial solutions included:

* Setting a set of generic “backup” default values to use in the instance when a new implant is added that is not in the implantdefaults.json.
** The team would have implemented Journey default values since the next new TKA implant to be used with CORI will most likely fall in the Journey implant family.
** Main Issue: If the next implant were NOT Journey, the default values displayed to the user would be evidently wrong.  This would also cause the definition of what these values represent to be wrong.
* Implement the concept of “Implant Families” (as determined by the implant name) and have “backup” default values specific to the implant family.
** Main Issue: There is no formal concept of Implant Families as defined in the IDB. Thus, the team would be making an assumption around what an implant family is without any formal guidance.
** Additional Issue: This still would not cover scenarios in which a new implant were added that does not fall into the existing implant design “families”, i.e. Journey, Legion, Genesis, etc. Along these same lines, this would not cover any test IDBs in which the implant names do not fall into these categories either.
* Calculate the preference values we can from the IDB for any new implant not present in the implantdefaults.json file.
** This would involve pulling existing code from intraop and using it in Launcher (fairly risky)
** Main Issue: This would introduce potential dependencies between the Software and the IDB that do not currently exist.
** Other Issues:
*** The calculated values would not be “true defaults” even if they would be close
*** There is no reasonable way to determine Tibia medial resection depth from this method so there would either need to be a missing value with additional logic to ensure the user edits this value before they can save a preference OR you would need to have some systematic way to choose a value (i.e. apply the lateral RD to also be the medial) which would be inherently wrong in some cases.



The best long term solution would likely be an IDB process update.  For instance, it could be required moving forward, to include the implant default values as part of the IDB and these values could be read directly by CORI to be used in SPP (and the implantdefaults.json would be eliminated).

The system does this by displaying a purple planned cut line (static), and a live orange cut plane line that moves as the tracked tool move.   When the two lines are displayed as coincident the position of the plate probe matches the planned cut (that’s the goal).

The issue is that when the difference between plate probe and planned cut is only fractions of a mm or degree it’s difficult for surgeons to know which direction they need to move the plate to achieve the plan.

summary: Improve functionality of Cori soft shutdown slider
description:
Created from bug 1701.  Description from Jeremy:

There's two separate issues here:

 1. It's easy for the slider control to lose track of progress.

 It is a known issue that the circle on the slider control resets if you release your finger or touch anywhere outside of the slider's interaction zone, but I don't know if users are aware that the state logic does not check for a CONTINUOUS slide gesture. Instead, it is only checking for an interaction on the far right of the slider. The slider control will always snap the slider to your current interaction point - so if you touched the slider in the middle, the circle will automatically be redrawn in the middle of the slider control.

 Even if the slider loses track of your progress, you can keep sliding along the control until you notice the circle snapping back to the location of your finger.

 This interaction was confirmed on DV03. I started dragging my finger on the left side of the slider, then moved it slightly above the slider. The circle followed my finger until I moved it above the slider, then it snapped to the left side of the slider. I then dragged my finger back down to the slider, and the circle snapped back to the current location of my finger.

 So, I was not able to observe DV03 having an issue with shutting down due to the gesture control for the shutdown slider. At the same time, I could understand that a user who was not familiar with how the slider works would have an issue if they continued to swipe the screen from the left every time it reset. This leads into the next issue.

 2. The power-off slider has a frustratingly-narrow interaction zone.

 This one is slightly harder to address. Talking with Natalie about our options, it looks like we are extremely limited by our choice of hardware - the 4D Systems display. 4D Systems developed a proprietary DIABLO16 graphics controller based around a virtual processor, which is optimized to execute compiled code written in a proprietary high-level language (4DGL). In short, we're tied to the 4D Systems IDE, build process, and particular interactions regarding the display.

 If we use the current slider control, an easy solution would involve increasing the width of the slider control (including the orange bar) to account for the increased interaction zone. This would look different from the other sliders, so we may need Marketing's input before proceeding with this option.

 Alternatively, Natalie believes we can develop a new slider control, but we would need to research how the other slider control was developed and make the adjustments accordingly. It may also involve replacing the volume and irrigation slider controls to make sure that all three look the same. It's certainly not a trivial task, but we don't know how much effort will be involved just yet.

A key consideration in developing RI.OS is that it must be possible to migrate from the current architecture to RI.OS in an incremental fashion.

The updates to the TKA application will begin the process of migrating CORI software applications to the new architecture.

This epic will track the plans to migrate the applications to leverage the ri.OS platform.

RI.OS software architecture is meant to replace the current CORI software architecture, in order to make application development, testing, and deployment faster, easier, and less complex. FAI is an acronym for Femoral-Acetabular Impingement and refers to an arthroscopic sports medicine procedure in which the hip joint it re-shaped with a bur to improve hip flexion and reduce pain in the hip joint.  This specific ticket describes the development of an application which will be executed with the Cori platform to treat FAI through navigated resection of the femur neck.   At a high level the FAI Nav application will include the following components:

* Software application which runs on the Cori console which includes UI & computation for tool calibration, guided image registration, and navigation of a cutting instrument. 
* Independent, mobile camera cart - During the FAI procedure the camera may need moved around the OR to maintain visibility with the tracked tools.  The cart mounted camera would make this difficult as the cart also houses the Cori console with handpiece, tablet, footpedal, tensioner cables running from it to the patient. 
* Collection Probe - Mechanical component used for characterization of the physical bone, necessary for image registration.  Analogous to the Cori Point Probe.  Will need to be tracked using the Cori tracking system.  
* Cutting Tool - Mechanical component used for shaping the patients bone.  Will likely be an existing sports-med cutting wand with a tracking frame attached.  This tool will need to be tracked using the Cori tracking system.  

Not included in this ticket is the development of an FAI Planning application which is necessary the deployment of an FAI but separate from the FAI Nav applicaiton.  The FAI Plan application will be run on a personal device (e.g. laptop or tablet), will use medical imaging and user interaction as input to create a resection plan to treat the patient specific case of FAI.  The plan that is the output of the ‘FAI Plan’ application will be the primary input for ‘FAI Nav’ application.

description:
Instruments required for use with an Active Arm procedure need to be provided in a sterilization tray that integrates into the CORI tray system and minimizes the number of trays required for a CORI procedure (this includes both CORI and manual knee system instruments).  

Active Arm Specific Instruments may include the following:

* End Effector (ie. saw, drill, or cut guide)
* End Effector Tracker
* End effector interface

CORI Instruments that may be required for an active arm TKA procedure may include:

* Point Probe
* Femur and Tibia Trackers
* Tracker attachment hardware

Manual Knee System Instruments that may be required for an active arm TKA procedure may include:

* Trial Implants
* Impactors and finishing instruments

The active arm contains both non-sterile hardware and instruments that can be sterilized.  The non-sterile hardware is required to be in the sterile field when in use.  In order to use the arm it must be covered in sterile disposable drape.

A leg stabilization method is not desired but may be required in order to ensure cut accuracy.  If a leg stabilization device is required for technical reasons then a solution should consider the following:

# Impact to surgical workfllow - Ease of assembly and restrictions to other steps (ie. hip center)
# Minimize additional cost - both COGS and sterilization

A mobile, compact and lightweight cart is needed to support the Active Arm during use as well as facilitate transportation throughout the hospital.  The footprint of the arm should be minimized so it does not interfere with the surgery.  

*Non Sterile Setup* - The system should guide the user through required setup steps and calibrations.  Where possible, the UI should clearly show the user what they need to do.  A non-sterile person should be able to complete as many of the setup tasks as possible

*Sterile Setup -* The cart should help facilitate the sterile draping and sterile instrument attachment process

*Operation* - During use the arm cart should not impede the operative flow of the surgeon, PA or scrub tech

*Removal from sterile field* - The arm should be able to be removed from the sterile field after its use is finished  in order to get it out of the way and prepare it for another surgery.

*Storage* - When not in use the combined footprint of the Arm Cart and the CORI Cart should be minimized in order to take up less space in a hospital closet or hallway.  Both carts should look like they belong together and ideally nest in order to minimize footprint.  A customized dust cover is desirable

*Transport within hospital* - A single person should be able to move the cart between operating rooms, hallways and storage closets within a hospital.  This includes going through standard doorways and elevators

*Shipping* - Shippable components should be below the maximum allowable size and weight of conventional shipping carriers (ie. Fedex and UPS).  Because the overall weight of the cart is likely to exceed the maximum weight, a modular design is desired

* The Active arm component is most likely to be required to be returned to a service center and therefore should be easily detachable from the support structure.  
* Electronics - It is likely that additional weight will be required for stability of the arm during operation.  Therefore, where possible, system electronics (ie. communications gateways, e-stop, manipulator electronics, UPS, transformer ect.) should be moved into the cart.  Electronics that are likely to require service should be modular and able to be removed from the support structure
* Support Structure and weight - Contains components that are field serviceable (ie. casters, cables, ect.)

summary: Collection of Post-Op ROM (proposed update to current algorithm)
description:
Currently CORI tracks the post-op ROM throughout the post-operative screens and ultimately displays the maximum extension and maximum flexion value detected by the system whenever trackers are visible. The value displayed on the case review screen is not representative of the footpedal captured data but of the max extension and max flexion seen by the trackers. 

There are various point in time when the trackers may be visible on the Femur and Tibia but there are not trial components in the joint, and this can lead to skewed reporting in the case review screen (i.e. extreme hyperextension)

We have received a number of questions and points of field feedback on this topic and would like to suggest we update the functionality of the software to be more representative of the information the surgeon is choosing to collect. Based on feedback, we would like to collect the post-op flexion range from last footpedal driven collection in the baseline state. This implementation is analogous in nature to our pre-op flexion range of motion collection (range of motion), and will allow the user to determine when and what range of motion is collected. 

This should eliminate skewed data visible on the case review screen. Moreover, this information will be transitioned to RI.INSIGHTS (data management platform) and can be referenced by the surgeon after cases are completed. 

Have attached the first FR, and there has been further feedback provided to the team, mainly from the ANZ market, but also from select US sites.
